title: When Threat Persists: Stress, Anxiety, and Recovery
takeaways: Sympathetic nerves, adrenal catecholamines, and the HPA axis operate through different structures and time courses; negative feedback helps limit glucocorticoid exposure.
The same learned danger can produce freezing, retreat, flight, or social avoidance; score the actual action and identify the setting before assigning a mechanism.
Vulnerability and exposure are separate stages.
Development, pre-existing anatomy, and later experience can each influence persistent symptoms; an anatomical difference measured afterward does not identify when it began.
Safe experience changes the expression of a learned prediction without necessarily deleting the original association; context and prior training affect later retrieval.
Relief can reinforce rituals, familiar actions can acquire value, and cell-specific striatal changes can promote repetition; ordinary grooming is not itself OCD.
Treatments act at different biological levels.

ERP changes learned expectations and ritual responding, reuptake inhibitors alter serotonin clearance, and stimulation changes network activity; evaluate clinical symptoms and functioning separately from animal circuit outcomes.
